intro.title: Types and class()
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Every value in R has a **type**, and the type decides what you can do with it. You can add numbers but not text; you can count TRUEs but not words. Most surprises in data analysis come from a value having a different type than you thought.

The four types you will meet all the time:

| Type | Examples | `class()` gives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| numbers with decimals | `4.5`, `-2`, `1e6` | `"numeric"` |
| whole numbers | `5L`, `1:3` | `"integer"` |
| text | `"kale"`, `"42"` | `"character"` |
| TRUE/FALSE | `TRUE`, `x > 3` | `"logical"` |

`class()` tells you the type of a value or a vector. Use it whenever something doesn't behave as you expect:

```
class(4.5)        # "numeric"
class("4.5")      # "character": the quotes make it text
class(1:3)        # "integer"
class(TRUE)       # "logical"
```

Plain numbers like `5` are "numeric", even without decimals. An `L` after a number (`5L`) makes an **integer**, a whole number stored as such. Sequences made with `:` are integers too. In practice numeric and integer work the same for maths.

There are also yes/no checks for each type: `is.numeric()`, `is.character()` and `is.logical()`. `is.numeric()` is TRUE for integers too.

Remember from the vectors quest: a vector holds one type. Mix types in `c()` and R picks the type that can hold everything: logical becomes numeric, and numeric becomes character. So `c(1, TRUE)` is `1 1`, and `c(1, "a")` is `"1" "a"`.

intro.title: Converting types
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Data often arrives as the wrong type. A spreadsheet column of prices might come in as text, or a code like `"007"` might come in as a number. The `as.` functions convert values:

| Function | Turns into | Example | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `as.numeric()` | a number | `as.numeric("4.5")` | `4.5` |
| `as.integer()` | a whole number | `as.integer(3.9)` | `3` |
| `as.character()` | text | `as.character(42)` | `"42"` |
| `as.logical()` | TRUE/FALSE | `as.logical("TRUE")` | `TRUE` |

They work on whole vectors, so one call fixes a whole column: `as.numeric(c("12", "8", "15"))` is `12 8 15`.

When a value can't be converted, you get `NA` and a warning, "NAs introduced by coercion". That is useful: it finds the values that aren't really numbers.

```
as.numeric(c("12", "8", "n/a", "15"))   # 12 8 NA 15, with a warning
```

Two surprises. `as.integer()` doesn't round, it cuts off the decimals: `as.integer(3.9)` is 3. And `as.logical()` understands `"TRUE"`, `"true"`, `"T"` and `"FALSE"`, but not `"yes"`, and turns the numbers 0 and 1 into FALSE and TRUE.

Converting to text and back loses nothing for simple numbers, but leading zeros vanish when text becomes a number: `as.numeric("007")` is 7. That's why codes such as postcodes or IDs should stay as text.

intro.title: Choosing with ifelse()
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`ifelse()` makes a new vector by choosing, value by value, between two answers. It takes a condition, the value to use where it is TRUE, and the value to use where it is FALSE:

```
scores <- c(71, 44, 88, 50, 39)
ifelse(scores >= 50, "pass", "fail")   # "pass" "fail" "pass" "pass" "fail"
```

Read it as "if the score is 50 or more, pass, else fail", done for every score at once. The answers can be numbers too, or even other vectors of the same length:

```
minutes <- c(12, 47, 30)
ifelse(minutes > 30, minutes * 0.15, 0)   # 0.00 7.05 0.00: pay only for long rides
```

For three or more groups, put one `ifelse()` inside another. R checks the first condition; where it is FALSE, it moves on to the inner `ifelse()`:

```
ifelse(scores >= 70, "high", ifelse(scores >= 50, "middle", "low"))
```

Where the condition is `NA`, the answer is `NA` too, so missing values stay missing. A common use is filling in gaps: `ifelse(is.na(x), 0, x)` replaces each NA with 0 and keeps the other values.

For many groups based on number ranges, `cut()`, two stages from now, is tidier than lots of nested `ifelse()`s.

intro.title: Factors
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Much data is a choice from a short, fixed list: a T-shirt size, a ticket type, a rating from "poor" to "great". R has a special type for this, the **factor**. A factor stores the values together with the list of allowed values, called its **levels**.

```
sizes <- factor(c("M", "S", "L", "M", "M"))
sizes
levels(sizes)    # "L" "M" "S"
```

R shows the values without quotes, then the levels underneath. By default the levels are sorted alphabetically, which is rarely the natural order. Give the order yourself with `levels =`:

```
sizes <- factor(c("M", "S", "L", "M", "M"), levels = c("S", "M", "L"))
levels(sizes)    # "S" "M" "L"
```

Why bother? The level order is used everywhere later: in counts, summaries and charts, S, M, L comes out in a sensible order instead of L, M, S. Levels also show categories that have no values yet, which matters when you count them.

A value that isn't one of the levels becomes `NA`, which catches typos: `factor(c("S", "XL"), levels = c("S", "M", "L"))` gives `S <NA>`. `nlevels()` counts the levels, and `as.character()` turns a factor back into plain text.

For categories that have a real order, such as ratings, use `ordered = TRUE`. Then comparisons work: `rating > "ok"` is TRUE for "good" and "great".

intro.title: Counting with table()
intro.bodyMarkdown:
"How many of each?" is one of the first questions you ask about any data. `table()` answers it: it counts how often each value appears.

```
drinks <- c("latte", "tea", "latte", "mocha", "latte", "tea")
table(drinks)
```

The result shows each value above its count: latte 3, mocha 1, tea 2. A table works much like a named vector, so you can pick a count by name, and `names()` gives the values:

```
counts <- table(drinks)
counts["latte"]       # 3
names(counts)         # "latte" "mocha" "tea"
```

Sort it to see the most common first: `sort(counts, decreasing = TRUE)`. The top value is then `names(sort(counts, decreasing = TRUE))[1]`.

`prop.table()` turns counts into **shares** of the total, which add up to 1. Multiply by 100 for percentages:

```
round(prop.table(counts) * 100)   # latte 50, mocha 17, tea 33
```

With a factor, `table()` uses its levels: in their order, and with a 0 for any level that never appears. That's often exactly what you want in a report. `table()` leaves out `NA`s unless you add `useNA = "ifany"`.

drinks <- c("latte", "tea", "latte", "mocha", "latte", "tea")
counts <- table(drinks)
counts
counts["latte"]
sort(counts, decreasing = TRUE)
round(prop.table(counts) * 100)

intro.title: Grouping numbers with cut()
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Sometimes you want groups instead of exact numbers: age bands, price ranges, short, medium and long rides. `cut()` sorts numbers into groups between **break points** and gives a factor:

```
ages <- c(8, 15, 34, 67, 41, 12)
cut(ages, breaks = c(0, 12, 17, 64, 120))
```

The groups are shown like `(12,17]`: the round bracket means "more than 12" and the square bracket means "up to and including 17". So a 12-year-old goes in `(0,12]` and a 13-year-old in `(12,17]`. A value outside all the breaks becomes `NA`, so make the first break low enough and the last high enough.

Readable names are better than brackets. Give one label per group with `labels =`, so there is always one label fewer than break points:

```
band <- cut(ages, breaks = c(0, 12, 17, 64, 120),
           labels = c("child", "teen", "adult", "senior"))
table(band)
```

Because the result is a factor, the groups keep their natural order in `table()` and later in charts, and empty groups still show with a 0.

If you'd rather include the lower end ("from 0 up to but not including 12"), add `right = FALSE`. The groups then look like `[0,12)`. Use `-Inf` and `Inf` as breaks for "anything below" and "anything above".

band <- cut(ages, breaks = c(0, 12, 17, 64, 120), labels = c("child", "teen", "adult", "senior"))
table(band)

intro.title: More text tools
intro.bodyMarkdown:
The first quest showed `paste()`, `nchar()` and `toupper()`. Here are the next tools, and like most of R they all work on whole vectors at once.

`substr(x, start, stop)` cuts out part of a text by character position: `substr("2026-10-30", 1, 4)` is `"2026"`. Handy for codes where each part sits in a fixed place.

`trimws()` removes spaces at the start and end, a very common problem in typed-in data: `trimws("  Ana ")` is `"Ana"`.

`strsplit()` splits a text into pieces at a separator. Because it can split several texts at once, it gives a **list** with one vector per text; take the first with `[[1]]`:

```
strsplit("tea,milk,sugar", ",")[[1]]   # "tea" "milk" "sugar"
```

`sprintf()` builds a text from a template, with a placeholder for each value. It is the way to show money with exactly two decimals:

| Placeholder | Means | Example | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `%s` | text | `sprintf("Hi %s", "Ana")` | `"Hi Ana"` |
| `%d` | whole number | `sprintf("%d cups", 3L)` | `"3 cups"` |
| `%.2f` | number with 2 decimals | `sprintf("%.2f", 9.6)` | `"9.60"` |
| `%5.1f` | 5 characters wide, 1 decimal | `sprintf("%5.1f", 3.14159)` | `"  3.1"` |

```
cat(sprintf("Total: %.2f\n", 9.6))      # Total: 9.60
```

`%d` needs a whole number. A plain number like `3` works too, but `3.5` gives an error; use `%.0f` or `round()` for those.

sprintf("%.2f", 9.6)

intro.title: Finding and replacing text
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`grepl(pattern, x)` asks, for each text, "does it contain this?", and gives TRUE or FALSE. Use it to pick out matching values, just like any other condition:

```
items <- c("oat latte", "black tea", "latte", "mocha", "chai latte")
grepl("latte", items)           # TRUE FALSE TRUE FALSE TRUE
items[grepl("latte", items)]    # the three lattes
sum(grepl("latte", items))      # 3
```

Matching is case-sensitive. Add `ignore.case = TRUE` to match "Latte" and "LATTE" too.

`sub(pattern, replacement, x)` replaces the **first** match in each text, and `gsub()` replaces **every** match ("g" for global):

```
gsub("-", " ", "2026-10-30")    # "2026 10 30"
sub("-", " ", "2026-10-30")     # "2026 10-30"
gsub(" ", "", "07 700 900 123")  # "07700900123": remove all spaces
```

The pattern is a **regular expression**, a small language for describing text. You only need a few pieces: `^` means "at the start", `$` means "at the end", `.` means "any character", and ` +` means "one or more spaces". So `grepl("^B", x)` finds texts starting with B, and `gsub(" +", " ", x)` turns runs of spaces into one.

Because `.` has a special meaning, replacing a real dot needs `fixed = TRUE`, which treats the pattern as plain text: `gsub(".", ",", "3.50", fixed = TRUE)` is `"3,50"`. `startsWith()` and `endsWith()` are simple alternatives for checking the start and end.

intro.title: Dates
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A date written as text, like `"2026-10-30"`, is just characters: you can't subtract it or add a week. `as.Date()` turns it into a real **Date**, which R understands:

```
borrowed <- as.Date("2026-10-02")
returned <- as.Date("2026-10-23")
returned - borrowed               # Time difference of 21 days
as.numeric(returned - borrowed)   # 21
```

`as.Date()` expects the year first: `YYYY-MM-DD`. Subtracting two dates gives a time difference; wrap it in `as.numeric()` to get a plain number of days. Adding a number adds days: `borrowed + 14` is the due date, two weeks later.

Dates can be compared and sorted like numbers: `returned > borrowed` is TRUE, and `sort()` puts dates in order. They also work in vectors, so one line handles a whole column of loans.

`format()` shows a date any way you like, using codes for its parts:

| Code | Gives | For 2026-10-30 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `%Y` | year | `2026` |
| `%m` | month number | `10` |
| `%d` | day of the month | `30` |
| `%B` | month name | `October` |
| `%A` | weekday name | `Friday` |

```
format(as.Date("2026-10-30"), "%d %B %Y")   # "30 October 2026"
weekdays(as.Date("2026-10-30"))              # "Friday"
```

Dates written another way can be read with a `format` too: `as.Date("30/10/2026", format = "%d/%m/%Y")`. And `seq()` makes date sequences: `seq(as.Date("2026-10-01"), by = "week", length.out = 4)` gives four Thursdays a week apart.

returned <- as.Date("2026-10-23")
returned - borrowed
as.numeric(returned - borrowed)
borrowed + 14

weekdays(returned)

intro.title: Lists
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A vector holds one type. A **list** can hold anything: numbers, text, whole vectors, even other lists. That makes it the natural way to keep different facts about one thing together, such as one library member:

```
member <- list(name = "Ana Silva", age = 34, loans = c("FI-104", "SC-221"), active = TRUE)
```

Get one item out with `$` and its name, or with double square brackets: `member$name` and `member[["name"]]` both give `"Ana Silva"`. `member$loans` gives the vector of loan codes, which you can then use like any vector: `length(member$loans)` is 2.

```
member$name
member[["age"]]
length(member$loans)
```

Single square brackets work differently: `member["name"]` gives a smaller **list** containing that item, not the item itself. When you want the value, use `$` or `[[ ]]`.

You can change an item or add a new one by assigning to it: `member$age <- 35`, `member$email <- "ana@example.org"`. `names()` lists the items and `length()` counts them.

Lists are everywhere in R once you look: `strsplit()` gives a list, and the data frames in the next quest are lists of columns that all have the same length. `str()` shows the structure of a list in a compact way.

member <- list(name = "Ana Silva", age = 34, loans = c("FI-104", "SC-221"), active = TRUE)
member$name
member[["age"]]
length(member$loans)

str(member)

intro.title: Easy side quest: The visitor survey
intro.bodyMarkdown:
The Riverside Library asked visitors one question on a paper form: "Would you come to an evening opening?" Volunteers typed the answers in, each in their own way:

```
answers <- c("Yes", "no", " yes", "YES", "No", NA, "yes ", "no")
```

To R, `"Yes"`, `" yes"` and `"YES"` are three different answers. Clean them up, count them, and report the result:

```
yes: 4
no: 3
Yes share: 57%
```

The share is of the people who answered, leaving out the blank form.

challenges.solution:

challenges.title: Expert: The survey report
challenges.promptMarkdown:
Starting from the messy answers, clean them and show:

```
yes: 4
no: 3
Yes share: 57%
```
challenges.hint: Clean with `tolower(trimws())`, count with `table()`, and build each line with `cat()`. `cat("Yes share: ", share, "%\n", sep = "")` leaves out the spaces.
challenges.solution:
answers <- c("Yes", "no", " yes", "YES", "No", NA, "yes ", "no")
clean <- tolower(trimws(answers))
counts <- table(factor(clean, levels = c("yes", "no")))
share <- round(counts[["yes"]] / sum(counts) * 100)
cat("yes:", counts[["yes"]], "\n")
cat("no:", counts[["no"]], "\n")
cat("Yes share: ", share, "%\n", sep = "")

challenges.title: Expert: The loans report
challenges.promptMarkdown:
Starting from the text dates, show:

```
Late: 2 of 5
Fines: 3.50
Busiest shelf: FI
```

Show the fines with two decimals. When two shelves tie, the one that comes first in the levels (`FI`, `SC`, `HI`) wins.
challenges.hint: Dates with `as.Date()`, days and `ifelse()` as before, `sprintf("%.2f", …)` for the fines, and `names(which.max(table(shelf)))` for the busiest shelf.
challenges.solution:
codes <- c("FI-104", "SC-221", "FI-350", "HI-007", "SC-118")
borrowed <- c("2026-10-01", "2026-10-03", "2026-10-07", "2026-10-10", "2026-10-12")
returned <- c("2026-10-12", "2026-10-25", "2026-10-21", "2026-10-30", "2026-10-20")
days <- as.numeric(as.Date(returned) - as.Date(borrowed))
days_late <- ifelse(days > 14, days - 14, 0)
shelf <- factor(substr(codes, 1, 2), levels = c("FI", "SC", "HI"))
cat("Late:", sum(days > 14), "of", length(days), "\n")
cat("Fines:", sprintf("%.2f", sum(days_late * 0.25)), "\n")
cat("Busiest shelf:", names(which.max(table(shelf))), "\n")

tests.assertion: identical(trimws(strsplit(._cq_stdout, "\n", fixed = TRUE)[[1]], "right"), c("Late: 2 of 5", "Fines: 3.50", "Busiest shelf: FI"))

intro.title: Hard side quest: The sign-up sheet
intro.bodyMarkdown:
The garden club had a sign-up sheet for its autumn workshop. People typed their own names, with stray spaces, odd capitals, and one person who signed up twice:

```
signups <- c("  ana SILVA", "Ben   okafor ", "cy LI", "ANA silva", "dee  Mensah")
```

Make a clean list of people, each name written properly once, plus their initials for the name badges. The last challenge shows:

```
4 people signed up
Ana Silva (AS)
Ben Okafor (BO)
Cy Li (CL)
Dee Mensah (DM)
```

You will need `trimws()`, `gsub()`, `tolower()`, `toupper()`, `substr()`, `sub()` and `unique()`, which gives each different value once.
intro.sandboxCode:
signups <- c("  ana SILVA", "Ben   okafor ", "cy LI", "ANA silva", "dee  Mensah")
trimws(signups)
gsub(" +", " ", trimws(signups))

challenges.title: Easy: Tidy spaces and capitals
challenges.promptMarkdown: Make `tidy` the names with no spaces at the ends, single spaces between words, and all small letters.
challenges.starterCode: signups <- c("  ana SILVA", "Ben   okafor ", "cy LI", "ANA silva", "dee  Mensah")
challenges.solution:
signups <- c("  ana SILVA", "Ben   okafor ", "cy LI", "ANA silva", "dee  Mensah")
tidy <- tolower(gsub(" +", " ", trimws(signups)))

tests.label: tidy is ana silva, ben okafor, cy li, ana silva, dee mensah
tests.assertion: identical(tidy, c("ana silva", "ben okafor", "cy li", "ana silva", "dee mensah"))

challenges.title: Medium: Each person once

challenges.starterCode: signups <- c("ana silva", "ben okafor", "cy li", "ana silva", "dee mensah")

signups <- c("ana silva", "ben okafor", "cy li", "ana silva", "dee mensah")

challenges.title: Expert: The badge list
challenges.promptMarkdown:
Starting from the messy sign-ups, show:

```
4 people signed up
Ana Silva (AS)
Ben Okafor (BO)
Cy Li (CL)
Dee Mensah (DM)
```
challenges.starterCode: signups <- c("  ana SILVA", "Ben   okafor ", "cy LI", "ANA silva", "dee  Mensah")
challenges.hint: Tidy, `unique()`, split into first and last, add capitals, then `cat(sprintf("%s %s (%s%s)\n", First, Last, …), sep = "")` shows one line per person.
challenges.solution:
signups <- c("  ana SILVA", "Ben   okafor ", "cy LI", "ANA silva", "dee  Mensah")
people <- unique(tolower(gsub(" +", " ", trimws(signups))))
first <- sub(" .*", "", people)
last <- sub(".* ", "", people)
First <- paste0(toupper(substr(first, 1, 1)), substr(first, 2, nchar(first)))
Last <- paste0(toupper(substr(last, 1, 1)), substr(last, 2, nchar(last)))
cat(length(people), "people signed up\n")
cat(sprintf("%s %s (%s%s)\n", First, Last, substr(First, 1, 1), substr(Last, 1, 1)), sep = "")

tests.label: Shows the badge list
tests.assertion: identical(trimws(strsplit(._cq_stdout, "\n", fixed = TRUE)[[1]], "right"), c("4 people signed up", "Ana Silva (AS)", "Ben Okafor (BO)", "Cy Li (CL)", "Dee Mensah (DM)"))

`.* ` matches everything up to and including the space.
